nameStory: The "Great Piddock" gets its name from the Old English word "piddoc," meaning to bore or pierce. These remarkable clams earned this title by literally drilling holes into solid rock and wood using their shells like living power tools, creating permanent burrows where they spend their entire adult lives.
description: The Great Piddock is a large, white clam that lives by boring perfectly round holes into rocks, wood pilings, and clay banks along New England's coast. Unlike typical clams that burrow in sand or mud, these engineering marvels use their ridged shells to grind through solid materials. They can grow up to 6 inches long and create burrows that extend several inches deep into their chosen substrate. Once they've carved out their home, they're stuck there for life, filtering food from water that flows through their tunnel.

idTips.label: Rock-boring lifestyle
idTips.description: Look for perfectly round holes about 1-2 inches wide in rocks, wooden pilings, or clay banks near the waterline - these are piddock burrows with the clam living deep inside

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: The white shell feels rough and raspy like coarse sandpaper, especially on the front end where rows of tiny ridges act like a natural file for boring

idTips.label: Siphon tubes
idTips.description: Two fleshy tubes extend from the burrow opening - one darker tube sucks in water while a lighter one expels waste and filtered water

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: The elongated shell tapers to a point at the front (boring end) and gapes open at both ends, feeling fragile and thin compared to typical clams

idTips.label: Size and depth
idTips.description: Mature specimens can reach 6 inches long, living in burrows that extend 8-12 inches deep into solid substrate

habitat: Great Piddocks live in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in softer rocks like shale, sandstone, and clay banks. You'll find their characteristic round holes in wooden pier pilings, harbor structures, and natural rock formations from Maine to Connecticut. They prefer areas with good water circulation where they can filter-feed effectively from their permanent burrows.

seasonality.spring: Siphon activity increases as water warms, making the tubes more visible extending from burrow holes during low tide. This is peak feeding season as plankton blooms provide abundant food.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with siphons frequently extended during low tides. Best time to observe their feeding behavior and spot the dual tubes pumping water in tide pools and rocky areas.
seasonality.fall: Siphon activity decreases but shells may wash up after storms, showing their distinctive boring ridges and gaping shape. Good time to examine empty shells on beaches.
seasonality.winter: Least active period with siphons rarely visible, but burrow holes remain obvious in rocks and pilings. Ice and storms may expose or damage shallow burrows.

funFact: Great Piddocks can actually glow in the dark! When disturbed, they produce a bright blue-green bioluminescent light from their siphons and the inside of their burrows - early settlers sometimes used them as natural lanterns, and the light is bright enough to read by.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other boring clams, but Great Piddocks create the largest, most perfectly round holes. Remember: "Great size, great holes" - their burrows are noticeably bigger and more circular than those made by smaller boring clams or marine worms.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their "clam" classification, piddocks are quite different from typical clams you might harvest for food. Their shells lack the hinge ligament that holds normal clam shells together, instead being held in place by their tight burrow. They're also not typically eaten due to their boring lifestyle and thin shells.
compareHints: Great Piddocks are the only Zirfaea species in New England waters. Compared to other piddock family members like the smaller Angel Wings, Great Piddocks are significantly larger, bore deeper holes, and have more pronounced rasping ridges on their shells. Their burrows are also more perfectly circular and larger in diameter than those of related boring clams.
